bivy.name: Lake Ann
bivy.capacity: Established sites scattered around the lake and its outlet
bivy.water: The lake itself, reliable all season — the last dependable water before the climb
bivy.permit: No national park backcountry permit needed here; the lake sits outside the park boundary, and the Price zone permit applies only to camps higher on the route
bivy.notes: A comfortable planned camp about four miles in, reached by a short spur off the climbers' path at the saddle. It is the easy, low-commitment option and the one most parties use, but it leaves the whole talus traverse and the 4th-class chimneys for summit day, and a returning party has to re-gain roughly a thousand feet over the saddle to get back to the car.

bivy.name: Top of the Chimneys rock outcrop
bivy.capacity: A handful of small bivy spots on and around the outcrop
bivy.water: Meltwater pools at the base of the outcrop; seasonal, and unreliable once the snow above has gone
bivy.permit: Backcountry permit for the Price cross-country zone (max party 12, six parties per night)
bivy.notes: A planned bivy for parties splitting the route, sitting on dry ground just past the top of the chimney system near the edge of the upper glacier. Everything you sleep in has to be carried up a thousand feet of 4th-class scrambling to get here, and going down in bad weather means reversing that same braided ledge system, which is easy to lose in cloud.

bivy.name: Rock rib above Winnie's Slide
bivy.capacity: Room for about three tents; several more single bivy spots reported along the rib
bivy.water: A stream or waterfall running off the rib, seasonal and dependent on snow above
bivy.permit: Backcountry permit for the Price cross-country zone (max party 12, six parties per night)
bivy.notes: The highest and best-positioned planned camp, on dry ground on a narrow spur bordering the Upper Curtis Glacier, with the summit day cut down to the glaciers and the summit pyramid. It is also the most committing: it is above the steep snow and ice of Winnie's Slide, so a party that has to bail in a storm must down-climb or rappel that before touching the chimneys. Exposed to wind, and the flat ground is small enough that a late arrival may find it taken.

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites scattered along the moraine crest roughly between 5,800 and 6,200 ft; exactly where parties end up depends on where the water is running and who arrived first
bivy.water: Running meltwater at camp, but nothing above it — carry everything you need for the summit day from here, and treat it
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, two to three hours up from the trailhead on the moraine beside the Coleman Glacier. It is above the trees, so there is nothing to hang food from and nothing to break the wind coming off the glacier; the rock-walled spots are there for a reason. Reach it early in the day if you can — the three creeks on the approach are fed by glacial melt and run noticeably higher and pushier through the afternoon.

bivy.name: Kulshan Cabin site
bivy.capacity: A few sites at the old cabin clearing
bivy.water: Creeks along the trail nearby; treat all of it
bivy.notes: A lower fallback just below treeline where the cabin used to stand. Nothing remains of the structure, but there are trees for shelter and for hanging food, which Hogsback does not have. Worth knowing about as a foul-weather retreat rather than as a first choice, since it leaves another thousand feet of climbing before the glacier.

bivy.name: Mountaineer Creek basin (beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers)
bivy.capacity: Several established gravel and heather sites in the hanging valley
bivy.water: The south fork of Mountaineer Creek runs through the basin, plus snowmelt; reliable through the season
bivy.notes: The standard planned base camp for the north-side approach, and the last flat, sheltered ground with running water. Getting here means leaving the maintained trail before Stuart Lake, crossing the creek and following it cross-country for roughly two miles, then climbing a steep loose talus slope — the crossing runs high and fast in early season. From camp it is another four to five hours to the base of the ridge. Overnight camping on this side may fall inside the quota'd permit area for the range; check which zone your intended site is in before committing to sleeping here.

bivy.name: The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
bivy.capacity: Two genuinely good bivy spots, plus a number of mediocre ones nearby
bivy.water: None reliable — seasonal snow patches only, and nothing at all once they melt out
bivy.notes: The classic place to split the complete ridge, reached by the snow-filled gully (usually climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) above the Stuart Glacier. This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, but only two spots are actually comfortable and a party of three or more will be spread out. Wind-scoured and fully exposed, with no water above it, so the summit day starts with everything you carried.

bivy.name: Goat Pass
bivy.capacity: Numerous good bivy sites on the pass
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns early to mid season; Ingalls Creek is the reliable source, below the pass
bivy.notes: The camp for the southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek — a longer, higher-gain walk in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop because the Cascadian Couloir descent drops back the same way. A planned camp with plenty of flat ground, though water becomes a carry once the snow patches are gone.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shore and around the south end; busy and competitive on summer weekends
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season
bivy.permit: An overnight permit for the lake's zone in the quota'd wilderness permit area is required from mid-May through October and is one of the harder ones to draw; outside that window permits are free and unlimited
bivy.notes: The planned base camp for the route, roughly two and a quarter hours from the trailhead. Camp as close to the south end as you can — everything you save there is time you are not walking in the dark, because the moraine above the lake still adds about a thousand feet before the first pitch. The permit difficulty is why a great many parties simply climb the route in a single push from the car instead.

bivy.name: First large flat ledge low on the ridge
bivy.capacity: One ledge, big enough for a party of two to sit out a night
bivy.water: None — everything must be carried
bivy.notes: An emergency bivy, not a camp. It is the first genuinely flat spot after the initial pitches and is normally used as a break and gear-sorting stance, but it is somewhere to stop if a party is benighted low on the ridge. There is no water, no shelter and no easy way off from here, so treat it as a place to survive a night rather than a planned stage.

bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.capacity: 110 people overnight; the public shelter sleeps roughly 25-30 on a first-come basis and the rest is tent ground
bivy.water: None running — every drop is melted snow, so plan fuel accordingly
bivy.permit: A wilderness camping permit is required and the camp is quota'd, plus a climbing permit for anyone travelling on glaciers or above about 10,000 ft. Roughly half the camp's capacity is held back for walk-up registration in summer
bivy.notes: The planned high camp for the route, on the saddle between the snowfield and the Cowlitz Glacier, with a ranger station and toilets. It is the most sheltered option on this side of the mountain and the public hut is the fallback when a storm makes tents impractical, though the hut is cold and drafty. Rangers here give the forecast before summit attempts. Nothing about it is quiet or private on a summer weekend.

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.capacity: 35 people overnight; tent camping only, no structures
bivy.water: Melted snow only
bivy.permit: Wilderness camping permit required and quota'd separately from the camp below, plus the climbing permit
bivy.notes: A planned camp that takes a thousand feet off summit day, and the reason parties accept the trade-offs. It has no toilet, so all solid waste is packed out. Large crevasses ring the flat ground — stay roped any time you leave the tent platforms. It also sits directly beneath the seracs of the icefall above; that slope is where an icefall killed eleven climbers in 1981, and parties keep their time in the fall line short.

bivy.name: Boulder Basin
bivy.capacity: Several established sites on heather and rock benches at treeline, spread through the basin between roughly 5,500 and 6,000 ft
bivy.water: Waterfalls and snowmelt streams run through the basin; dependable into late summer but shrinking as the season goes on. Filter it
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is required for overnight use in this wilderness
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a forested ridge with a full pack. It is about ten miles from the road end, and the road itself has a long history of washouts, so confirm where the trailhead actually is before you plan the day.

bivy.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
bivy.capacity: A small forested site or two just north of the trail junction
bivy.water: Sitkum Creek
bivy.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard camp.

bivy.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
bivy.capacity: Popular established riverside sites
bivy.water: The river and its tributaries
bivy.notes: The lowest planned stop, about 5.5 miles in and still widely used. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Useful as a first night for parties splitting the approach, or as a retreat in bad weather, but it is a long way and a lot of gain below the glacier.

bivy.name: Eldorado Creek Basin
bivy.capacity: Open camping on rock and gravel benches — no built pads; the zone allows six parties a night, twelve people to a party
bivy.water: Eldorado Creek and snowmelt through the basin, reliable
bivy.permit: A national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, reservable in advance and picked up at the ranger station in Marblemount
bivy.notes: The usual first camp, about three miles and 3,300 ft from the car and the first flat, pretty ground after the long climb through timber and the boulder field. Camp on durable surfaces only — snow, rock or bare ground — and stay a hundred feet back from water; the meadow here is exactly what the rule is protecting. A comfortable planned camp, and the natural choice for parties who reach it late in the day.

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin
bivy.capacity: Open camping on the rib and in the basin, between roughly 6,100 and 6,400 ft
bivy.water: Reliable running water in the basin
bivy.permit: Same national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone
bivy.notes: A higher alternative to the basin below, reached by climbing to the rocky ridge near 6,100 ft and dropping a few hundred feet down the far side. That drop has to be re-gained on the way out, which is the main argument against it, but it puts you closer to the glacier toe with water still running. A planned camp, not a bivy.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier saddle high camp
bivy.capacity: Flat glacier apron and rock beside it, roughly 7,500-7,800 ft; the zone limit of six parties a night applies
bivy.water: Snowmelt only — bring a stove, there is nothing running at this height
bivy.permit: Same national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone. A composting toilet serves this camp; if you sleep away from it, human waste must go into blue bags and come out with you
bivy.notes: The best-positioned planned camp, on the broad flat apron where the glaciers meet, with the East Ridge and the summit knife-edge laid out in front of you. It is entirely exposed — no trees, no shelter, and weather arrives with nothing in the way. Both the Eldorado and the Inspiration carry real crevasse hazard that gets worse as the day warms, so you rope up before you reach camp and again when you leave it.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites, four people to a site, four parties a night
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns at the glacier toe early to mid season; many of these dry up by late summer, so a late-season party should expect to melt snow or carry water up from lower down
bivy.permit: A national park backcountry permit is required and the camp is strictly quota'd — an early-access lottery runs in March and roughly 40% of permits are held for walk-ups, picked up at the wilderness information centre in Marblemount
bivy.notes: A planned camp and one of the highest in the park, where the maintained trail ends: flat gravel tent pads built onto rock mounds at the foot of the glacier, each ringed by a primitive dry-stone wall, plus a composting toilet. Those walls are there because the site is completely exposed to wind and weather with nothing above it. About six miles and 3,600 ft from the trailhead, and it puts the glacier and the summit pyramid within a short morning.

bivy.name: Doubtful Lake
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camping area in the basin
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season
bivy.permit: A national park backcountry permit is required
bivy.notes: The lower fallback, roughly a mile and a thousand feet down a signed spur off the arm. It has water when the high camp does not and it is far more sheltered in bad weather, at the cost of re-gaining that thousand feet to rejoin the route. Worth knowing because there is no camping permitted anywhere along Sahale Arm between the pass and the high camp — if you cannot get a high-camp site, this basin is the alternative rather than the next flat spot you find.
